newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan army offensive said to displace expatriates. [CORRECTED 11:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Angolan army offensive said to displace expatriates. [CORRECTED 11:00 GMT]

text.p: The Angolan army's offensive in the country's northeast has displaced up to 5,500 people, expatriates working in the region said on Friday.
(Corrects to make clear reference to people in general, not only expatriates).

"There are at least 4,000 displaced people in Nzaji," one said, referring to a government-held town in Angola's Lunda Norte province. "But there are another 1,500 in a camp about 20 km (12 miles) away from Nzaji and more people are arriving there every day."

The army offensive into UNITA-held diamond areas in the northeast started on May 18. Diplomats and military analysts in Luanda say the offensive is the biggest in over two yers and has resulted in some fierce clashes between the army and the former UNITA rebels.

UNITA, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, and the government fought a two-decade-long civil war that stopped only when the two sides signed a peace agreement in the Zambian capital Lusaka in 1994.

In April UNITA entered into a power-sharing arrangement with the government and over 60 of the movement's members took up their seats in the country's National Assembly. But UNITA continues to control vast areas of the Angolan countryside, including most of the richest diamond mining zones.

Residents in the area and displaced arriving from the south of Nzaji told expatriates the army now controls most of the district of Cambula, Angola's most northeastern district, sandwiched between the Chiumbre River and the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire.

"The people arriving on Thursday in Nzaji said the army was in control south of Maludi," said an expatriate, referring to a town in the southern part of the district. "They were all afraid and said some towns had changed hands a couple of times between the FAA (Angolan army) and UNITA."
The government has said the military movements in the northeast are designed to protect Angola from former members of the Zairean and Rwandan armies who are trying to enter the country.

UNITA says the offensive is being carried out against a civilian population, saying they have no way of fighting because the former rebels have complied with a U.N.- sponsored demobilization process and no longer have an army.
